name: Grindr
tagline: Location-based dating and hookup app for gay, bi, trans and queer people.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The software here is a grid of profile photos sorted by distance, a chat system, and some filters. All of that is a weekend, maybe less. The product is the several million people already standing inside it within walking distance of you, which is not a thing you can npm install. A self-hosted clone with one user is a mirror, and a self-hosted clone with nine friends is a group chat with worse UX. Also worth noting: this category carries real safety, moderation, and outing risk, so a hobby build with a leaky database is not a neutral outcome.
coreLoopDIY: A self-hosted proximity grid where invited members post a profile, see nearby members sorted by distance, and chat, with no discovery beyond your invite list.
requirements: A server with HTTPS and a real domain
Image storage and resizing for profile photos
Geolocation permission from every member's browser
Some plan for moderation and abuse reports, even at ten users
A hard commitment to encrypting location data and not logging it
whatYouLose: The only thing that matters: everyone else nearby, right now
Travel mode, where the grid repopulates the second you land in a new city
Years of trust and safety work: blocking, reporting, screenshot limits, discreet app icons, unsend
Push notifications on iOS and Android without shipping a native app to two stores
Anonymity infrastructure, which is life-and-safety critical in countries where this app is a target
moatNotes: Density beats features. A dating grid is only useful at a saturation level no self-hosted instance will ever reach, and the incumbent's advantage compounds because everyone joins where everyone already is.
whyPeopleStillPay: Paid tiers buy you more of the network, not more software: more profiles loaded, better filters, seeing who viewed you, fewer ads. That is the tell. Nobody is paying for the chat engine or the distance sorting, they are paying for deeper access to a crowd that took fifteen years to assemble in every city on earth. You cannot self-host a crowd.
notes: You can clone the grid in a weekend and it will be empty forever. The moat is millions of people already inside it within a five minute walk, plus a decade of safety tooling built for users who get arrested for being on it.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted, invite-only proximity directory and chat for a small private group. Be honest with me in the README that this is not a dating app replacement, it is a tool for a closed group that already knows each other.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js (App Router, TypeScript) with Tailwind
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, single file at ./data/app.db
- Auth: invite codes only, no signup form. Admin generates codes from a CLI script. Session via signed httpOnly cookie, secret in .env
- Photo upload to local disk ./data/uploads, resized with sharp to a 640px square, EXIF stripped (including GPS, this is not optional)
- Realtime chat via a single WebSocket server route, messages persisted in SQLite

Features in scope:
- Profile: display name, short bio, up to 3 photos, optional tags
- Location: browser geolocation, posted manually by a "update my location" button, never in the background. Store rounded to 3 decimal places
- Grid view: profiles sorted by haversine distance, distance shown bucketed ("under 1 km", "1-5 km", "5+ km"), never as an exact number or a bearing
- 1:1 chat with unread counts
- Block and report: blocking hides both directions immediately; reports write to an admin table
- Every user can delete their account and all photos and messages, with one button that actually works

Out of scope, do not build: payments, ads, push notifications, native apps, public discovery, search by exact location, read receipts, any analytics or telemetry, any third-party SDK.

Security requirements: rate limit login and message sends, validate all uploads by magic bytes, set a strict CSP, no location or message content in server logs.

Deliver: the app, a seed script with 5 fake users, a CLI script for invite codes, and a README that states plainly which risks a hobby deployment cannot cover.
